section_titles: Counting beyond 200
periods.activity_title: Counting the Mela: Guessing and Grouping in Tens

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Can you make a guess?, p.64
tasks_in_class.description: Guess the number of triangular torans in the mela picture.
Count all the triangular torans by grouping in tens to verify the total.
Guess how many bangles there are in the picture.
Count the total number of bangles using Teji's counting strategy (groups of 10).
How many more triangles to make 300? How many bangles less than 300? Which is more: bangles or triangles?

time_bands.activity: Open the mela picture together. Each child writes a private guess for Can you make a guess?, p.64 ("Guess the number of triangular torans in the mela picture...."). Invite a few guesses aloud — celebrate the range without revealing the answer.

Children work in pairs on Now find out, p.64 ("Count all the triangular torans by grouping in tens...."). Each pair circles groups of ten on the picture and records a running total. Pairs share counts; the class agrees on the total.

Repeat the guess-then-count rhythm with Guess, p.65 ("Guess how many bangles there are....") followed by Try counting, p.65 ("Count the total number of bangles using Teji's counting strategy...."). Children use the grouping-in-tens method they just practised.

Class works through Let us Do, p.65 ("How many more triangles to make 300? How many bangles less than 300? Which is more...."). Children reason aloud: how many steps from 280 to 300, from 250 to 300. Toffee-counting tasks (Guess p.65 and Count and check p.65) are noted as additional practice for early finishers.

periods.teacher_notes: The grouping-in-tens strategy is the conceptual anchor here — children who count one-by-one often miscount beyond 200, so insist on circling groups before counting. A common error is stopping at 290 and writing '290' rather than continuing the count to reach 298 or 300; ask 'How many more to reach the next hundred?' to catch this. Additional practice: Guess p.65 (toffees) and Count and check p.65 may be used as homework or extension.
materials: Pencils and crayons for circling groups

section_titles: Sequences and number patterns on tiles
periods.activity_title: Tile Trails and Arrow Paths: Filling Number Sequences

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the empty tiles on Jojo's tiled path with the correct numbers (sequences around 211–216, etc.).
Fill in blanks with correct numbers in three arrow sequences: (a) 294–310, (b) 227–234, (c) 382–390.
Guess how many ants there are; count and check. Discuss why different children get different answers.

time_bands.activity: Write three numbers from a tile-path sequence on the board with gaps (e.g. 211, ___, 213, ___, ___). Ask children to whisper the missing numbers to a partner before calling on the class. Establish that each tile is one more than the last.

Children complete Let us Do Q1, p.66 ("Fill in the empty tiles on Jojo's tiled path....") individually, then compare with a neighbour. Draw attention to any sequence that crosses a tens boundary (e.g. 219→220) and ask what happens to the tens digit.

Children tackle Let us Do Q2, p.66 ("Fill in blanks in three arrow sequences: (a) 294–310, (b) 227–234, (c) 382–390...."). Sequence (a) is the richest because it crosses from the 290s into 300s; invite a child to explain why 299+1 = 300.

Whole-class guess-and-count with Let us Do Q3, p.66 ("Guess how many ants; count and check. Discuss why different children get different answers...."). Children guess, then count by grouping in tens. Ask: why do some children get a different number? Lead the discussion toward consistent grouping as the reliable strategy.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have been grouping in tens to count large collections will find the tile sequences natural; the conceptual stretch here is crossing hundred boundaries (299→300) where both tens and hundreds digits change together. A common error is writing '200' or '399' when the sequence reaches the next hundred — ask the child to count on aloud from 297, 298, 299 to make the transition explicit. In Q3, different answers from different children open the door to discussing why a systematic method (grouping) is more reliable than random counting.

section_titles: Matchstick bundles and number sentences
periods.activity_title: Matchstick Bundles: Hundreds, Tens, Ones in Pictures and Words

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks: for each matchstick picture write the number and number sentence; for '300 and 16 more' and '109' draw matchsticks and complete the row.
Place the numbers from Q4 on the number line (0–350).

time_bands.activity: Draw a simple matchstick-bundle picture on the board: 2 large bundles (hundreds), 3 medium bundles (tens), 5 single sticks (ones). Ask children to call out what they see, then build the number sentence together: 200+30+5 = 235. Repeat with a number that has zero tens (e.g. 204) so children see an empty tens column.

Children work on Let us Do Q4, p.67 ("Fill in the blanks: for each matchstick picture write the number and number sentence; for '300 and 16 more' and '109' draw matchsticks...."). The reverse direction — given a number sentence, draw the bundles — is the richest task; circulate and check drawings for correct bundle sizes.

Children complete Let us Do Q5, p.67 ("Place the numbers from Q4 on the number line 0–350...."). Model placing one number together: count up from 0 in hundreds, then in tens, then in ones to find the approximate spot. Children place the remaining numbers and compare placements with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: The bridge between the concrete matchstick picture and the symbolic number sentence is the core move of this section — children who can read a picture but cannot write the expanded form may be treating hundreds, tens, and ones as labels rather than values (200, not '2'). A common error in the number-line task is placing 316 and 309 at the same position; ask the child to count in tens from 300 to locate each correctly. Emphasise that '300 and 16 more' means 316, not 3016.

section_titles: Number slider: increase and decrease by 1, 10, 20
periods.activity_title: Spin the Slider: Changing Digits One Place at a Time

tasks_in_class.description: Look at six matchstick pictures and write the corresponding 3-digit numbers.
Make the number slider; use it to increase/decrease: (a) 285+1, (b) 147+10, (c) 367−2, (d) 289−10, (e) 290+20.

time_bands.activity: Children open to p.68 and complete Let us Do Q6, p.68 ("Look at six matchstick pictures and write the corresponding 3-digit numbers....") independently. After writing, pairs check each other. Highlight any picture with zero tens, reinforcing the place holder.

Guide children to construct the number slider following the textbook instructions — cut the H, T, O strips and thread them through the card window. Once sliders are ready, set the starting number 285 together and ask: if we move only the ones wheel by one, what changes?

Children work through Let us Do Q7, p.68 ("use the slider to increase/decrease: (a) 285+1, (b) 147+10, (c) 367−2, (d) 289−10, (e) 290+20...."). After each calculation, they record the result. Pause at (d) 289−10=279 and (e) 290+20=310 to discuss which digit wheels turned and why.

periods.teacher_notes: The number slider makes visible what abstract arithmetic hides: only the relevant digit wheel moves when adding or subtracting ones or tens. A common error is changing the wrong wheel (e.g. moving hundreds instead of tens when adding 10); before each calculation, ask the child to point to the wheel they will move. For 290+20, children may also try to move only the tens wheel and discover that it overflows into the hundreds wheel — use this moment to show why the hundreds digit must change.
materials: Thick paper or card for slider strips

section_titles: Flag game: guessing a hidden number
Magical Count and extending hundreds on a number line
periods.activity_title: Flag Guesses and Magical Chains: Numbers on a Line

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Play — Flag game, p.69
tasks_in_class.description: Play the flag guessing game with a friend: one thinks of a number between 200 and 210, the other guesses using flag direction clues on the number line.
Write any number name, count its letters, write the name of that new number, keep repeating — what happens? Try with 187 and 204 as well.
Tell what the next hundred number is after 300; write it on the number line (0–400) and show it using matchsticks.

time_bands.activity: Children pair up for Let us Play — Flag game, p.69 ("one thinks of a number between 200 and 210, the other guesses using flag direction clues...."). Demonstrate one round on the board: write a number line from 200 to 210, mark a guess, and show the flag pointing left (too big) or right (too small). Each pair plays at least two rounds, swapping roles.

Introduce Magical Count, p.70 ("Write any number name, count its letters, write the name of that new number, keep repeating...."). Children start with their own chosen number. After a few steps, pause and ask: where does everyone end up? Repeat with 187 and 204 as directed, recording the chains.

Children work on Numbers on a line, p.70 ("Tell what the next hundred after 300 is; write it on the number line 0–400 and show it using matchsticks...."). They draw 4 bundles of 100 matchsticks on their page, confirm the number name 'four hundred', and mark 400 on the line, placing 100, 200, 300 first.

periods.teacher_notes: The flag game builds the same number-line reasoning students used when grouping in tens to count accurately — the position of a number relative to its neighbours is determined by comparison, not enumeration. A common error in the Magical Count activity is miscounting the letters in a number name (e.g. counting spaces or hyphens); model letter-by-letter counting with a pointer for 'two hundred and four'. For the number-line extension, children who already know that 100, 200, 300 are evenly spaced will quickly see 400 falls one more equal step to the right.

section_titles: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
periods.activity_title: Sweet Shop Numbers: Locating and Comparing on a Number Line

tasks_in_class.description: Locate 216, 243, 257 on the number line (200–260).
Locate 329, 332, 337, 375 and 387 on the number line (320–390).
Tell how far 387 is from 400 using the number line.
Which is more: 393 or 400? Use a number line and show by jumping how far 393 is from 400.
How many pieces of mysore pak are in one tray?

homework.description: How many pieces of mysore pak are there in total?
How many laddoos does chacha have in the trays?

time_bands.activity: Children complete Let us Do Q1, p.71 ("Locate 216, 243, 257 on the number line 200–260....") and Let us Do Q2, p.71 ("Locate 329, 332, 337, 375 and 387 on the number line 320–390...."). Model one placement: count up from the left end in tens to find the nearest ten below, then move in ones. Compare a few placements on the board.

Class works on Let us Do Q3, p.71 ("Tell how far 387 is from 400....") and Let us Do Q4, p.71 ("Which is more: 393 or 400? Show by jumping how far 393 is from 400...."). Ask children to draw the jumps explicitly — one jump of 10 from 387 to 397, then three ones — so the distance is made visible, not computed abstractly.

Introduce Farooq Chacha's sweet shop. Children read the tray picture carefully and complete Let us Do Q5(a), p.72 ("How many pieces of mysore pak are in one tray?..."). Discuss how counting groups of 100 is the same grouping-in-tens strategy applied to larger groups. Remaining sweet-shop sub-questions (b)–(g) are set as homework or additional practice.

periods.teacher_notes: The number-line placement tasks draw on the same grouping-in-tens reasoning children used to count large collections; the new demand is deciding how far apart to draw each ten-jump on the line. A common error is placing 387 and 375 at equal distances from 370 — ask the child to count the tick marks between 375 and 387 to see the gap is 12, not equal. For Q5(a), children who try to count sweets individually rather than reading the tray label 'each tray holds 100' benefit from being redirected to the picture caption.

section_titles: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
periods.activity_title: Filling the Trays: Sweet Shop Problems and the 500 Number Line

tasks_in_class.description: How many dhoklas does chacha have?
Chacha is going to fill the tray with more laddoos. How many more laddoos will make the tray full?
How many total laddoos will he have after the last tray is full?
Mark 423, 487, 438, 476 on the number line (413–500); also mark Five Hundred (500).

time_bands.activity: Revisit the sweet shop picture from p.72 and confirm the tray sizes as a class. Ask: what does it mean to say a tray holds 100? Establish that counting trays is the same as counting hundreds — a quick show of hands: how many trays of dhokla are there?

Children work through Let us Do Q5(d), p.72 ("How many dhoklas does chacha have?"), Q5(e), p.72 ("How many more laddoos will make the tray full?"), and Q5(f), p.72 ("How many total laddoos after the last tray is full?...") in sequence. Pause after each to share answers; write the number sentence on the board (e.g. 100 − 67 = 33 more laddoos needed).

Children complete Let us Do Q5(g), p.72 ("Mark 423, 487, 438, 476 on the number line 413–500; also mark Five Hundred...."). This is the first number line extending to 500; model identifying the halfway point (around 456) first, then place numbers on either side. Children label each point and compare positions with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: The sequence of sweet-shop problems moves from reading a count (how many dhoklas) to computing a complement (how many more to fill the tray) to combining totals — each step builds on counting groups of 100 as the base strategy. A common error in Q5(e) is adding the missing laddoos to the filled trays rather than finding the difference (100 − current count); drawing a tray with empty and filled cells on the board makes the complementary structure visible. The 0–500 number line in Q5(g) is the widest scale yet; children should place 500 first, then use equal spacing to locate the others.

section_titles: Hop Hundreds Home: apartment grid and place value
periods.activity_title: Apartment Adventures: Finding House Numbers in the Grid

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q1 (Hop Hundreds Home), p.73
tasks_in_class.description: Find the house numbers of the shaded houses without counting; fill in shaded boxes with correct house numbers.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q2 (Jump Joy Residency), p.74
tasks_in_class.description: Colour the houses to which Arvind Dada has to deliver sweets: 209, 228, 242, 258, 267, 276, 290, 315, 346, 367, 389, 395.
Write the floor and column number for each of: 13, 67, 106, 159, 192, 231, 245, 328, 380, 399.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the apartment grid on p.73. Ask: what number is house 01? Move one step right — what happens? Move one floor up — what changes? Establish the rules: each step right adds 1 (ones), each floor up adds 10 (tens). Then let children attempt Let us Do Q1, p.73 ("Find the house numbers of the shaded houses without counting....") individually.

Children work on Let us Do Q2, p.74 ("Colour the houses for delivery: 209, 228, 242, 258, 267, 276, 290, 315, 346, 367, 389, 395...."). For each number, they identify the hundreds (which block), the tens (floor), and the ones (column) before colouring. Circulate and check a few — does 209 land in column 9, floor 0 of the 200-block?

Children complete Let us Do Q3, p.75 ("Write the floor and column number for each of: 13, 67, 106, 159, 192, 231, 245, 328, 380, 399...."). This is the reverse task — given the house number, name the floor and column. Review answers together, focusing on numbers with a zero ones digit (380) and a zero tens digit (106).

periods.teacher_notes: The apartment grid makes the H-T-O structure of 3-digit numbers spatially explicit — the column is the ones digit, the floor is the tens digit, and the block of 100 is the hundreds digit. A common error is reading the floor counting upward from 0 and confusing it with the tens digit when the number crosses a hundred boundary (e.g. placing 192 on the floor for the 9 in 192 rather than checking which hundred-block it belongs to). Encourage children to split each number into H, T, O on paper before locating it in the grid.

section_titles: Hop Hundreds Home: apartment grid and place value
periods.activity_title: Who Am I? Riddles and Grid Patterns

tasks_in_class.description: Find and write house numbers in the blank spaces of the partial grid (given 12, 144, 238, 319); discuss how numbers change moving up/down and left/right.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q5 (Who am I? — card 1), p.75
tasks_in_class.description: Who am I? I have digits 9, 1 and 5. I am less than 200. I have 9 ones.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q5 (Who am I? — card 2), p.75
tasks_in_class.description: Who am I? I am a 3-digit number. I have only digits 4 and 0.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q5 (Who am I? — card 3), p.75
tasks_in_class.description: Who am I? I am greater than 300 but less than 400. I have no tens. My ones and hundreds digits are the same.

time_bands.activity: Children work on Let us Do Q4, p.75 ("Find and write house numbers in the blank spaces of the partial grid given 12, 144, 238, 319; discuss how numbers change moving up/down and left/right...."). After filling the grid, hold a discussion: 'What did you notice about moving right? About moving up?' Draw out the +1 (right) and +10 (up) rules explicitly.

Read the first 'Who am I?' riddle aloud together — Let us Do Q5 card 1, p.75 ("I have digits 9, 1 and 5. I am less than 200. I have 9 ones...."). Think aloud: which digit must be in the ones place? Which goes in hundreds? Solve together, then let children work on cards 2 and 3 individually, writing their reasoning before revealing the number. Share and discuss differing answers.

periods.teacher_notes: The partial grid in Q4 rewards the generalisation children built in the previous unit — each step right adds 1, each floor up adds 10 — now applied in reverse to fill in missing values. A common error in the 'Who am I?' riddles is using the same digit in the wrong place (e.g. putting 9 in the hundreds column for card 1, violating 'less than 200'); encourage children to eliminate impossible arrangements systematically before committing to an answer. Card 3 ('no tens, ones and hundreds the same') is the richest: write all H-_-O possibilities with H=O to narrow the field.

section_titles: Dienes blocks: drawing H-T-O for 3-digit numbers
periods.activity_title: Drawing the Boxes: Dienes Blocks for Sweet-Shop Numbers

tasks_in_class.description: Draw Dienes block representations for house numbers 309, 275, 423, 365, 343, 458, 562, 606, 800; write types of boxes/packets and number sentence.

time_bands.activity: Introduce Arvind Dada's packing system on p.76. Draw a box of 100, a box of 10, and a single sweet on the board. Ask: if I need to pack 235 sweets, how many of each box do I use? Build the picture together: 2 large boxes + 3 medium boxes + 5 singles, and write 200+30+5=235 beneath it.

Children work through Let us Do Q6, p.76 ("Draw Dienes block representations for 309, 275, 423, 365, 343, 458, 562, 606, 800; write types of boxes and number sentence...."). Circulate and pay close attention to 309 (zero tens box) and 606 (zero tens again) — children often draw a small box where none should appear.

Bring the class together to compare drawings for 309 and 800. For 309: 3 large boxes + 0 medium boxes + 9 singles — what does the number sentence look like? (300+0+9 or 300+9.) For 800: only 8 large boxes, nothing else. Discuss how the Dienes picture and the number sentence match each digit's place value.

periods.teacher_notes: The Dienes block drawing is the most explicit symbolic-concrete bridge in the chapter, directly mapping each digit of a 3-digit number to a physical quantity of boxes. A common error is drawing a tens box for the zero in 309 or 606 — children may feel that leaving a column empty looks 'wrong'; reinforce that 0 tens means no medium box at all, and the number sentence has no tens term (or writes +0). For 800, some children try to draw 8 individual small boxes thinking of 8 singles rather than 8 hundreds; ask them to check against the number name 'eight hundred'.

section_titles: Number hunt, patterns, and 100-10 relationships
periods.activity_title: Patterns in the Grid, Packing Hundreds, and the Clap-Snap-Pat Game

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q7(a) (Spring Leap Homes), p.77
tasks_in_class.description: Write the house numbers of the yellow and pink houses in the Spring Leap Homes grid.
Write the pattern you see in the yellow and pink house numbers.
How many boxes of 10 fit in: (a) 1 box of 100, (b) 2 boxes of 100, (c) 4 boxes of 100, (d) one opened box of 100?
Play Clap-Snap-Pat: record hundreds (clap clap), tens (snap), ones (pat) in the table; given 211 is done, record four more numbers.

homework.book_ref: Let us Do Q9 (Number hunt), p.78
homework.description: Write all numbers between 200 and 300 that have 5 as a digit (Is 245 one such number? Write the others).

time_bands.activity: Children complete Let us Do Q7(a), p.77 ("Write the house numbers of the yellow and pink houses....") by reading the Spring Leap Homes diagonal grid. They then write the pattern they notice in Q7(b), p.77 ("Write the pattern you see in the yellow and pink house numbers...."). Ask two or three children to read their pattern description aloud; draw out the diagonal rule.

Children work on Let us Do Q8, p.77 ("How many boxes of 10 fit in 1 box of 100, 2 boxes, 4 boxes, one opened box?..."). Start with the physical image: if one big box holds 100 sweets and a medium box holds 10, how many mediums fill one big? Record the pattern (10, 20, 40) and ask children to predict the next term.

Play Let us Play — Clap-Snap-Pat, p.78 ("record hundreds as clap, tens as snap, ones as pat; given 211 is done, record four more numbers...."). The teacher calls a number; children respond with the correct body movements, then record the movements in the table. Swap — a child calls a number and classmates respond.

periods.teacher_notes: The Spring Leap Homes diagonal reveals that numbers on a diagonal increase by 11 each step (one ten and one one together) — a pattern that connects back to the +10 floor rule and +1 column rule children discovered in the apartment grid. A common error in Q8 is answering 'one' for part (d) ('one opened box of 100'), thinking the question asks how many big boxes remain; clarify that the question asks how many medium boxes of 10 are now visible inside. Number hunt (Q9) is set as homework because listing all numbers from 200–300 with a 5 in any digit position is systematic and benefits from unhurried work.

section_titles: Number hunt, patterns, and 100-10 relationships
Comparing numbers using > and <
periods.activity_title: Show and Tell, Then Compare: Introducing > and <

tasks_in_class.description: Create a chain of cards: each card states a number and asks 'Who has …?'; distribute, read aloud, and identify the answer chain.
Compare using > or <: (a) 199 and 201, (b) 285 and 275.
Think and match: link each comparison statement (a)–(f) to the correct reason (six pairs).
Make all 3-digit numbers using digits 3, 2, 4 without repeating; colour the greatest red and smallest yellow.

time_bands.activity: Run the Show and Tell, p.78 ("Create a chain of cards: each states a number and asks 'Who has …?'; distribute, read aloud, identify the chain...."). Prepare a set of 10–12 cards (teacher-made from the textbook's model, using numbers in the 200–400 range). Children take turns reading and responding, forming a human chain around the room.

Introduce the > and < symbols using the laddoo story from p.79. Draw two Dienes block pictures on the board (487 and 423 as in the book). Ask: which is bigger? How do you know? Establish the hundreds-first rule. Children then complete Let us Do Q1, p.79 ("Compare using > or <: (a) 199 and 201, (b) 285 and 275....") and Let us Do Q2, p.80 ("Think and match: link each comparison statement to the correct reason....").

Children work on Let us Do Q5, p.81 ("Make all 3-digit numbers using digits 3, 2, 4 without repeating; colour greatest red, smallest yellow...."). Model a systematic listing strategy: fix the hundreds digit, then vary tens and ones. Children list all six numbers, then identify the greatest and smallest. Q7(a) is set as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The Show and Tell card game consolidates H-T-O reading in a social, playful format before the comparison section demands that same reading in a more analytical way. A common error when introducing > and < is applying the rule only to the first digit regardless of its place value — a child may say '285 > 275' correctly but then say '99 > 199' because '9 > 1'; insist on naming the hundreds digit first every time. In Q5, children who list only some of the six arrangements benefit from the fix-the-hundreds-digit strategy: start with 3__, then 2__, then 4__.
materials: Pre-cut number chain cards (teacher-prepared using numbers from the textbook's Show and Tell model)

periods.activity_title: Hundreds, Tens, Ones: Bringing the Whole Chapter Together

tasks_in_class.description: Make more 3-digit numbers using 3, 2, 4 allowing repeats; colour the greatest red and smallest yellow.
Arrange from biggest to smallest: 67, 376, 294, 249, 494.

time_bands.activity: Open with a rapid whole-class circuit: the teacher calls a 3-digit number (e.g. 347) and children hold up fingers to show hundreds (3), then tens (4), then ones (7). Move through five numbers spanning 200–500, mixing numbers with zero tens (e.g. 305) and round hundreds (e.g. 400). This activates the H-T-O decomposition that runs through matchstick bundles, Dienes blocks, the number slider, and the apartment grid.

Children work on Let us Do Q6, p.81 ("Make more 3-digit numbers using 3, 2, 4 allowing repeats; colour greatest red, smallest yellow...."). Because repetition is now allowed, the range of numbers is much larger. Ask: what is the greatest possible 3-digit number using these digits? What is the smallest? Connect to the comparison strategy — hundreds first — that was used to compare laddoo counts, sequence tiles, and apartment house numbers throughout the chapter.

Children complete Let us Do Q7(b), p.81 ("Arrange from biggest to smallest: 67, 376, 294, 249, 494...."). This set deliberately includes a 2-digit number (67) alongside 3-digit numbers — children must decide where it belongs. Bring the class together to share their ordered lists and debate any disagreements, using the hundreds-first comparison rule as the arbiter. Close by asking children to name one number they found easy to place and one that surprised them, connecting their reasons back to what hundreds, tens, and ones each tell us.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit weaves together every representation and strategy from the chapter: grouping in tens to count, matchstick and Dienes block decomposition, the number-slider logic for changing one digit at a time, apartment-grid place-value reading, number-line distance reasoning, and the hundreds-first comparison rule. A common error when ordering mixed 2- and 3-digit numbers is placing 67 above 200-range numbers because '6 looks big' — use the Dienes block image to show that 67 has no hundreds box at all. Encourage children to narrate their reasoning aloud as they order, using the vocabulary hundreds, tens, and ones throughout.

Arrange from smallest to biggest: 456, 389, 207, 99, 110.
Chacha is going to fill the tray with more laddoos. How many more laddoos will make the tray full?
How many total laddoos will he have after the last tray is full?

items.section_title: Counting beyond 200
items.prompt: There are 23 groups of 10 bangles and 4 loose bangles. How many bangles are there in all? Write the total and explain how you counted.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 234 bangles. 23 groups of 10 = 230, plus 4 loose = 234.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the groups of ten first, then add the loose ones.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw 23 circles each labelled '10' and count on; confident students may try a starting number like 27 groups and 6 loose and repeat the method.

exercise.description: Count all the triangular torans by grouping in tens to verify the total.

items.section_title: Number slider: increase and decrease by 1, 10, 20
items.prompt: A number slider shows 265. Riya moves only the tens wheel one step up. What number does the slider show now?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 275. Moving the tens wheel one step up adds 10 to 265.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 10 to the tens digit only; hundreds and ones stay the same.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student moved the ones wheel instead of the tens wheel, adding 1.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student moved the hundreds wheel instead of the tens wheel, adding 100.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student subtracted 5 from the ones, confusing increase with rounding down.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may act out the move with a hand-made slider (three strips of paper); confident students may try: what starting number gives 300 after one tens-wheel step up?

exercise.description: Make the number slider; use it to increase/decrease: (a) 285+1, (b) 147+10, (c) 367−2, (d) 289−10, (e) 290+20.

items.section_title: Dienes blocks: drawing H-T-O for 3-digit numbers
items.prompt: Draw Dienes blocks for the number 304. Write how many hundred-boxes, ten-boxes, and single pieces you used. Then write the number sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 hundred-boxes, 0 ten-boxes, 4 single pieces. Number sentence: 300 + 4 = 304.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read each digit of 304 as H=3, T=0, O=4 and draw the matching blocks.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may write the digits 3, 0, 4 above three blank columns and fill one column at a time; confident students may draw blocks for 406 and explain why the tens column is empty there too.

exercise.description: Draw Dienes block representations for house numbers 309, 275, 423, 365, 343, 458, 562, 606, 800; write types of boxes/packets and number sentence.

items.section_title: Number hunt, patterns, and 100-10 relationships
items.prompt: Priya has a card that says: 'I have 248. Who has the number that is 10 more?' Which card answers Priya's question?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 258. Adding 10 to 248 changes only the tens digit: 4 tens becomes 5 tens.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 10 by increasing the tens digit by 1; hundreds and ones stay the same.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added 1 instead of 10, changing the ones digit.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 100 instead of 10, changing the hundreds digit.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student subtracted 10 instead of adding, getting 10 less.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a number slider or write the H-T-O columns for 248 and change only T; confident students may be asked: what card would answer 'Who has 10 less than 248?'

exercise.description: Create a chain of cards: each card states a number and asks 'Who has …?'; distribute, read aloud, and identify the answer chain.

items.section_title: Counting beyond 200
items.prompt: There are 287 torans at the mela. How many more torans are needed to make exactly 300? How did you find your answer?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 13 more torans. Count on from 287: 287 → 290 is 3 more, 290 → 300 is 10 more; 3 + 10 = 13.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count on in steps from 287 to the next ten, then to 300.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may count on one-by-one from 287 to 300; confident students may try: if there were 293 torans, how many more to reach 300?

exercise.description: How many more triangles to make 300? How many bangles less than 300? Which is more: bangles or triangles?

items.section_title: Sequences and number patterns on tiles
items.prompt: Two children count the same group of ants. Seema gets 43 and Raj gets 47. Give one reason why their answers might be different, and explain what they could do to get the same answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: They may have counted some ants twice or missed some. Grouping in tens first — circling each group of ten — makes counting reliable and gives everyone the same total.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Group objects in tens before counting so that no object is counted twice or missed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may simply say 'they made a mistake'; prompt them with: what could they do differently? Confident students may be asked: if there are exactly 4 groups of 10 and 6 loose ants, what is the total? Who is closer, Seema or Raj?

exercise.description: Guess how many ants there are; count and check. Discuss why different children get different answers.

items.section_title: Matchstick bundles and number sentences
items.prompt: A matchstick picture shows 2 big bundles (hundreds), 0 medium bundles (tens), and 6 single sticks (ones). Which number sentence matches this picture?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 200 + 6 = 206. Two big bundles = 200, zero medium bundles = 0 tens, six singles = 6 ones.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read each bundle size as its place value: big = hundred, medium = ten, single = one.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student treated the 6 single sticks as 6 tens (60) rather than 6 ones.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student ignored the big bundles and treated the picture as a 2-digit number.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student wrote 06 as 6 tens, conflating the notation with the meaning.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw three columns (H, T, O) and fill in the counts before writing the sentence; confident students may be asked to draw the matchstick picture for 307 and write its number sentence.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks: for each matchstick picture write the number and number sentence; for '300 and 16 more' and '109' draw matchsticks and complete the row.

items.section_title: Flag game: guessing a hidden number
items.prompt: Meena thinks of a number between 200 and 210. You guess 205 and the flag points right (too small). You guess 208 and the flag points left (too big). What numbers could Meena's number be? Write all possibilities.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 206 or 207. The number is greater than 205 (flag points right) and less than 208 (flag points left), so it must be 206 or 207.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use each clue to eliminate numbers: greater than 205 removes 200–205; less than 208 removes 208–210.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may cross out numbers on the number line one clue at a time; confident students may be asked: what single guess would you make next to find the exact number in one try?

exercise.book_ref: Let us Play — Flag game, p.69
exercise.description: Play the flag guessing game with a friend: one thinks of a number between 200 and 210, the other guesses using flag direction clues on the number line.

items.section_title: Magical Count and extending hundreds on a number line
items.prompt: Arjun starts the Magical Count with the number FIFTY. He counts the letters (5), writes FIVE, counts again (4), writes FOUR, counts again (4), writes FOUR… Where does the chain always end?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: FOUR. The word FOUR has exactly 4 letters, so counting its letters gives 4 again — the chain loops forever at FOUR.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the letters in each number name; FOUR is a fixed point because it has exactly 4 letters.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have stopped one step too early, before reaching FOUR from FIVE (FIVE→5→FIVE loops or →FOUR; confusion about which number comes after FIVE in the chain).
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student stopped at FIVE, not noticing that FIVE (4 letters) leads to FOUR (4 letters) next.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have been thinking of 10 as a 'round' ending number rather than following the letter-count rule.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may write the letters of each word and count them with a finger; confident students may try starting with a very long number name like TWO HUNDRED AND FOUR and verify they still reach FOUR.

exercise.description: Write any number name, count its letters, write the name of that new number, keep repeating — what happens? Try with 187 and 204 as well.

items.section_title: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
items.prompt: Look at the number line from 380 to 400. The number 387 is marked on it. How many steps of 1 does it take to jump from 387 to 400?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 13 steps. From 387 to 390 is 3 steps; from 390 to 400 is 10 steps; 3 + 10 = 13.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump to the next ten first (387→390 = 3), then jump in tens to 400 (390→400 = 10); add the jumps.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may count forward one-by-one from 387 to 400 on the number line; confident students may be asked to find how many steps from 376 to 400.

exercise.description: Tell how far 387 is from 400 using the number line.

items.section_title: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
items.prompt: Which is more, 396 or 400? How many jumps of 1 on the number line take you from 396 to 400?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 400 is more; 4 jumps. 400 has 4 hundreds; 396 has only 3. Count on from 396: 397, 398, 399, 400 — that is 4 steps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare hundreds first (400 > 396), then count on from 396 to 400.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student counted from 394 or confused 'distance' with the ones digit of 396.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student incorrectly placed 396 as greater, perhaps reading '96' as bigger than '00' without checking hundreds.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confused jumping in tens with jumping in ones, arriving at 40 steps.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw a number line from 395 to 401 and count marks; confident students may be asked: how many jumps of 10 from 360 to 400?

exercise.description: Which is more: 393 or 400? Use a number line and show by jumping how far 393 is from 400.

items.section_title: Hop Hundreds Home: apartment grid and place value
items.prompt: In an apartment building numbered like Hop Hundreds Home, house 145 is on floor 4, column 5. Without counting every house, write the house number directly above 145 (one floor up) and the house number directly to the right of 145 (one step right). Explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One floor up: 155 (adding 10). One step right: 146 (adding 1). Moving up one floor adds 10 to the tens digit; moving right one step adds 1 to the ones digit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the apartment grid rules: up = +10, right = +1.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw a small grid fragment around 145 and fill in a few neighbours; confident students may be asked: what house is two floors up and three steps right of 145?

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q1 (Hop Hundreds Home), p.73
exercise.description: Find the house numbers of the shaded houses without counting; fill in shaded boxes with correct house numbers.

items.section_title: Hop Hundreds Home: apartment grid and place value
items.prompt: I am a 3-digit number. I am greater than 300 but less than 400. I have no tens. My ones digit and my hundreds digit are the same. What number am I?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 303. Hundreds digit = 3 (since the number is between 300 and 400). Tens digit = 0 (no tens). Ones digit = hundreds digit = 3. So the number is 303.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fix hundreds = 3, tens = 0 from the clues, then set ones = hundreds = 3.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may write _ _ _ and fill in each position from the clues in order; confident students may be asked to make up their own 'Who am I?' riddle with a different 3-digit number.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q5 (Who am I? — card 3), p.75
exercise.description: Who am I? I am greater than 300 but less than 400. I have no tens. My ones and hundreds digits are the same.

items.section_title: Number hunt, patterns, and 100-10 relationships
items.prompt: Arvind Dada opens 3 boxes of 100 sweets each. He wants to repack them into boxes of 10. How many boxes of 10 will he fill completely?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 30 boxes of 10. Each box of 100 = 10 boxes of 10; 3 boxes of 100 = 3 × 10 = 30 boxes of 10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the 100 = 10 × 10 relationship: multiply the number of hundred-boxes by 10.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student kept the count of hundred-boxes unchanged, not converting to ten-boxes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student found only how many boxes of 10 fit in ONE hundred-box, ignoring the other two.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confused the total number of sweets (300) with the number of ten-boxes needed.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw 3 large boxes, each split into 10 smaller boxes, and count all small boxes; confident students may be asked: how many boxes of 10 fit in 4 boxes of 100?

exercise.description: How many boxes of 10 fit in: (a) 1 box of 100, (b) 2 boxes of 100, (c) 4 boxes of 100, (d) one opened box of 100?

items.section_title: Comparing numbers using > and <
items.prompt: Riya says 289 > 312 because the digit 8 is bigger than the digit 1. Is Riya correct? Write whether she is right or wrong and explain using the hundreds-first rule.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Riya is wrong. Compare hundreds first: 289 has 2 hundreds and 312 has 3 hundreds. Since 3 > 2, we know 312 > 289, no matter what the tens or ones digits are.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the hundreds digit first; if they differ, the number with the greater hundreds digit is larger.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw Dienes block pictures for both numbers and count the hundred-boxes; confident students may be asked: write another pair of numbers where looking at only one digit would give the wrong comparison.

exercise.description: Think and match: link each comparison statement (a)–(f) to the correct reason (six pairs).

items.section_title: Comparing numbers using > and <
items.prompt: Using the digits 1, 5, and 8 (each used once), write all six possible 3-digit numbers. Circle the greatest number in red and the smallest in yellow.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The six numbers are: 158, 185, 518, 581, 815, 851. Greatest: 851 (circle red). Smallest: 158 (circle yellow).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fix the hundreds digit, then arrange the other two digits in both orders; repeat for each hundreds digit.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may write the digits on three separate slips of paper and physically arrange them; confident students may be asked: if you could repeat a digit, what would the greatest possible number be?

exercise.description: Make all 3-digit numbers using digits 3, 2, 4 without repeating; colour the greatest red and smallest yellow.

items.section_title: Sequences and number patterns on tiles
items.prompt: A tile path reads: 297, 298, 299, ___, 301. What number belongs in the blank tile?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 300. Each tile is one more than the last: 299 + 1 = 300.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 1 to the previous tile number to find the next.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student went backwards by 9, possibly misreading the sequence direction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student added 10 instead of 1, confusing a tens-step with a ones-step.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have placed 399 by confusing the hundreds digit when crossing into 300.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may count on aloud from 297; confident students may be asked to fill a tile path that crosses from 399 to 401.

exercise.description: Fill in blanks with correct numbers in three arrow sequences: (a) 294–310, (b) 227–234, (c) 382–390.

items.section_title: Matchstick bundles and number sentences
items.prompt: A number line goes from 0 to 350. Place the following numbers on it by marking each with a short line and its label: 109, 200, 316. Describe in one sentence how you decided where to place 316.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 109 is placed just past the first hundred (between 100 and 200, closer to 100). 200 is placed exactly at the second tick. 316 is placed a little past 300, about halfway to 350. For 316: it is 16 steps past 300, so it sits between 300 and 350, closer to 300.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Locate the nearest hundred first, then count on in tens to find the approximate position.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may mark only the hundreds (100, 200, 300) first and then place each number in its gap; confident students may be asked to also place 255 and explain their reasoning.

exercise.description: Place the numbers from Q4 on the number line (0–350).

items.section_title: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
items.prompt: Mark the numbers 431, 465, and 490 on the number line below. Write one sentence explaining how you found the position of 465.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 431 is placed between 420 and 440, 11 steps from 420. 465 is placed between 460 and 480, 5 steps from 460. 490 is placed between 480 and 500, 10 steps from 480. For 465: it is 5 ones past 460, so it sits just after the 460 mark.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the nearest ten on the line, then count on in ones to place the number.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may first mark every ten (420, 430, 440…) and then count ones; confident students may be asked to also mark 500 and check that 490 is exactly 10 steps away.

exercise.description: Mark 423, 487, 438, 476 on the number line (413–500); also mark Five Hundred (500).

items.section_title: Number hunt, patterns, and 100-10 relationships
items.prompt: Write all numbers between 300 and 400 that have the digit 5 somewhere. (Hint: 5 could be in the ones place, the tens place, or — could it be in the hundreds place? Think carefully.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Numbers between 300 and 400 with digit 5: 305, 315, 325, 335, 345, 350, 351, 352, 353, 354, 355, 356, 357, 358, 359, 365, 375, 385, 395. The hundreds digit is 3 for all, so 5 appears only in the tens or ones place. (355 has 5 in both tens and ones — accept it.) The hundreds digit cannot be 5 for numbers between 300 and 400.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fix hundreds = 3; search systematically: first all 3_5 numbers (ones = 5), then all 35_ numbers (tens = 5).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may write numbers from 300 to 400 in a column and circle those with a 5 digit; confident students may be asked how many such numbers there are in total (19).

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q9 (Number hunt), p.78
exercise.description: Write all numbers between 200 and 300 that have 5 as a digit (Is 245 one such number? Write the others).

items.section_title: Comparing numbers using > and <
items.prompt: Arrange these numbers from smallest to biggest: 342, 88, 421, 234, 89.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 88, 89, 234, 342, 421. The two 2-digit numbers (88, 89) come first because they have no hundreds; among 3-digit numbers, compare hundreds first: 2 < 3 < 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place 2-digit numbers first (no hundreds), then order 3-digit numbers by hundreds digit.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student placed 89 after 234, not recognising that a 2-digit number is always smaller than a 3-digit number.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student arranged from biggest to smallest instead of smallest to biggest.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly placed 88 and 89 first but then reversed 234 and 342.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may write each number's digit count first and sort by length before comparing; confident students may be asked to also place 400 in the correct position in the ordered list.

exercise.description: Arrange from smallest to biggest: 456, 389, 207, 99, 110.

items.section_title: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
items.prompt: A tray holds 100 laddoos. Chacha already has 73 laddoos in the tray. How many more laddoos does he need to fill the tray completely?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the current count from 100: 100 − 73 = 27.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw a tray of 100 squares, shade 73, and count the empty squares; confident students may change the count to 68 and solve again.

exercise.description: Chacha is going to fill the tray with more laddoos. How many more laddoos will make the tray full?

items.section_title: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
items.prompt: Chacha has 2 full trays of laddoos with 100 in each, and a third tray with 65. After he fills the third tray completely, how many laddoos does he have in total?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 300 laddoos. 2 full trays = 200; third tray filled = 100; total = 200 + 100 = 300.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count full trays as hundreds, then add: 200 + 100 = 300.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw 3 tray boxes and fill each to 100 before adding; confident students may be asked: if chacha had 4 trays with 85 each and fills them all, how many laddoos in total?

exercise.description: How many total laddoos will he have after the last tray is full?
